source: Koriat (1997) Monitoring one's own knowledge during study: a cue-utilization approach to judgments of learning
finding: Founding cue-utilization theory. Judgments of learning (JOLs) are inferences from cues, not a direct read of memory. Three cue types: intrinsic (item difficulty), extrinsic (learning conditions such as repetition and study time) and mnemonic (internal feedback such as ease of learning). Extrinsic cues are under-weighted. With practice, JOL shifts from intrinsic cues to mnemonic heuristics.
numbers: 4 paired-associate experiments. Item difficulty moved JOL about as much as recall. Repetition and stimulus duration moved JOL less than recall. Practice raised underconfidence (worse calibration) but improved resolution (better recall-JOL correlation).
limits: Abstract only (via OpenAlex); the PDF could not be text-extracted this session. Per-experiment N and gammas not recorded.
agent_relevance: Confidence is a cue-based inference. Our code should name which cue a confidence number rests on. Calibration and resolution must be measured separately because practice moved them in opposite directions.

source: Koriat, Ackerman, Lockl & Schneider (2009) The easily learned, easily remembered heuristic in children
finding: Mnemonic-cue heuristic 'easily learned, easily remembered' (ELER). Items needing more trials to acquisition (TTA) are recalled less, and JOLs follow the same rule, so the heuristic is valid and used. Children use it at ages 7 to 10. When all items are hard (restricted range), only 4th graders show the reliance. 2nd graders do not.
numbers: Exp1 N=40 (2nd and 4th grade): gamma(TTA, recall) -.74 (4th) and -.64 (2nd); gamma(TTA, JOL) about -.60 and -.56; gamma(JOL, recall) .56 (4th) and .68 (2nd). Exp2 N=60, hard pairs only: gamma(TTA, JOL) -.22 for 4th graders (significant) vs -.04 for 2nd graders (ns); gamma(TTA, recall) -.37 and -.31.
limits: Children and paired associates only. Learners' explicit estimates of their own TTAs correlated only about .43 with real TTAs, so the cue use is largely implicit.
agent_relevance: A monitoring cue is useful only when it is valid and the range is wide. Cues fail silently when all items look alike (restriction of range). Warn when a problem class gives no spread in the cue.

source: Koriat (1993) How do we know that we know? The accessibility model of the feeling of knowing
finding: Feeling of knowing (FOK) is computed from the amount of partial information that comes to mind while trying to retrieve, whether that information is correct or not. FOK is accurate because accessible partial information is mostly correct, not because a special monitor reads the memory trace.
numbers: 3 experiments (details not extracted). Koriat (2012) reports that the count of partial clues predicted recognition as well as the person's own FOK did.
limits: Abstract only (via OpenAlex), plus the secondary report in Koriat (2012).
agent_relevance: Evidence for G10: a report of knowing is a read-out of retrieval activity. A model's 'I know this' is only as good as the retrieval behind it. Count what was retrieved in code.

source: Koriat (2012) The self-consistency model of subjective confidence
finding: Main formal model of confidence. In a 2-alternative question a person draws a sample of representations and bases confidence on how consistently the chosen answer is supported across them. This is modelled on a statistical level of confidence. Confidence tracks consistency (reliability); calibration studies score it against correctness (validity). The confidence-accuracy link is a by-product of the consistency-correctness link. Response speed is a frugal cue to consistency, and accessibility (amount of information) adds an independent contribution.
numbers: Predictions confirmed across word matching, general knowledge, perceptual line comparison and other tasks: confidence rises with inter-person consensus and intra-person consistency for the majority choice and falls for the minority choice.
quote: Confidence monitors reliability (or self-consistency), but its accuracy is evaluated in calibration studies against correctness.
limits: Mostly 2-alternative forced choice. Item consensus needs a sample of other judges.
agent_relevance: For an LLM the analogue of consistency is agreement across independent samples. This supports counting sample agreement in code rather than reading a verbalised number. It also predicts failure where wrong answers are consistently favoured (G4).

source: Koriat (2012) Confidence-accuracy relation flips sign for consistently wrong items
finding: Direct demonstration of dissociation. Where most people choose the right answer (consensually correct, CC) confidence is higher for correct answers. Where most choose the wrong answer (consensually wrong, CW) confidence is higher for the wrong answer, so the confidence-accuracy correlation turns negative. Seen in word matching, general knowledge, and perceptual comparison.
numbers: Text states a within-person confidence-accuracy gamma of .47 on CC general-knowledge items and .24 on CW items, while also stating the correlation is negative for CW items in the aggregate figures; the two statements were not reconciled here. Sign flip also shown by item for consistently correct vs consistently wrong items (Figures 12E and 12F).
limits: CW items were deliberately included. How common they are in real use is unknown. The gamma figures should be re-read in the figure panels before reuse.
agent_relevance: Warning for G4 and G10: where the model's systematic error is the favoured answer, higher agreement and higher confidence point to the wrong answer. Agreement is not proof. A check on something the answer was not fitted to (G3) is needed.

source: Koriat (2012) Overconfidence as a reliability-validity gap, matched item sets
finding: Overconfidence shrinks or flips when confidence is scored against self-consistency instead of correctness. 36 matched items per task, first presentation only, 7 confidence categories (50 to 100).
numbers: Scored against accuracy: overconfidence 12.4 points (general knowledge) and 15.9 points (perceptual). Against item consensus: underconfidence 3.38 and 5.21 points. Against response consensus: overconfidence 6.78 and 4.59 points. Against repetition of own answer: underconfidence 12.80 and 7.05 points.
limits: Two tasks, one research programme. The reference index chosen changes the sign of the bias, so the account is partly definitional.
agent_relevance: Part of the 'overconfidence' we measure in LLMs may be a reliability-validity gap. Sample agreement is a better-behaved signal than the stated number but is still not a correctness signal.

source: Koriat (2012) Hard-easy effect in the self-consistency model, and the dispute over item selection
finding: Hard-easy effect: overconfidence falls as items get easier and flips to underconfidence on easy sets. Gigerenzer et al. and Juslin say it comes from selecting tricky items. Braun and Yaniv (1992), Griffin and Tversky (1992) and Soll (1996) found it with representative sets. The self-consistency model predicts a U-shaped confidence-accuracy function when items span 0 to 100% correct, because consensus rises as accuracy moves away from 50%.
numbers: Koriat (2008b) data fit the U shape (Figure 14). Review passage, no pooled N.
limits: Review passage inside a model paper; the cited studies were not opened.
agent_relevance: Calibration depends on difficulty mix. Do not fit one calibration map across easy and hard problems. Condition on a difficulty estimate (G12).

source: Gigerenzer, Hoffrage & Kleinbolting (1991) Probabilistic mental models: a Brunswikian theory of confidence
finding: PMM theory: people answer from cues valid in their environment and confidence is the validity of the best cue. Overconfidence and the hard-easy effect come from item selection that is unrepresentative. Predicts the confidence-frequency effect (single-item confidence exceeds the estimate of how many answers in a set are correct).
numbers: Two experiments. From a secondary search summary: selected item sets were hard (53% and 56% correct) and representative sets easier (72% and 75%); overconfidence vanished on representative sets.
limits: Abstract via OpenAlex; the numbers come from a secondary snippet and are unverified. Later work (Brenner et al. 1996, Griffin and Tversky 1992) found overconfidence even with representative samples.
agent_relevance: Calibration is relative to an item distribution. Test the agent on a representative sample of its real problems, not on hand-picked hard ones.

source: Juslin, Winman & Olsson (2000) Naive empiricism and dogmatism in confidence research: a critical examination of the hard-easy effect
finding: Quantitative review of 2-alternative general-knowledge studies. Most of the hard-easy effect comes from scale-end effects, linear dependency and regression to the mean, not from a cognitive bias. Representative and selected item samples differ in overconfidence beyond difficulty.
numbers: Secondary snippet (not verified): 95 selected-sample data points had mean confidence .73 against .64 correct; 35 representative-sample points had .73 against .72 correct.
limits: Abstract via OpenAlex; numbers from a search summary. Only 2AFC general knowledge. Contested by Griffin and Tversky (1992) and Brenner et al. (1996).
agent_relevance: Competing explanation: part of any hard-easy pattern is statistical. When we bin LLM calibration by difficulty, check regression to the mean first.

source: Moore & Healy (2008) The trouble with overconfidence
finding: Three kinds of overconfidence: overestimation of own performance, overplacement relative to others, and overprecision. On hard tasks people overestimate performance but underplace themselves. On easy tasks the reverse. Overprecision is the most persistent.
numbers: Theory plus experiments (figures not extracted).
limits: Abstract only (via OpenAlex).
agent_relevance: Log three things separately: is the stated probability too high, is the stated range too narrow, is the rank against other attempts wrong.

source: Kruger & Dunning (1999) Unskilled and unaware of it
finding: Low scorers overestimate. The unskilled lack the same skill needed to judge their own work (a double burden). Training raised metacognitive accuracy.
numbers: 4 studies (humor, grammar, logic). Bottom quartile scored at the 12th percentile and estimated the 62nd.
limits: Abstract only. Regression to the mean and the better-than-average effect can produce part of the pattern.
agent_relevance: When the monitor is the same model as the generator, the weakest cases are where its self-judgement is worst. A reason the monitor must be code or an independent check (G5).

source: Nelson & Dunlosky (1991) When people's judgments of learning are extremely accurate at predicting subsequent recall: the delayed-JOL effect
finding: Discovery of the delayed-JOL effect. A JOL made on the stimulus cue alone, some time after study, predicts later recall far better than a JOL made right after study. Previously JOLs had almost never been very accurate.
numbers: Gamma values not read this session (abstract says 'extremely accurate').
limits: Abstract only. The delayed cue-only judgment invites a covert retrieval attempt.
agent_relevance: Monitoring improves when the judge first tries to retrieve and then rates. For the agent: attempt cold, then rate, not rate in the same breath as generating.

source: Dunlosky & Nelson (1994) Does the sensitivity of JOLs to study activities depend on when the JOLs occur?
finding: Immediate JOLs are insensitive to how study activity changes memory. Delayed JOLs are sensitive: they rate interactive imagery above rote rehearsal and distributed above massed repetition, as recall does. Delayed JOLs are more polarised and more accurate item by item in every condition tested.
numbers: Two experiments. Gamma(JOL, recall) by condition: immediate roughly +.10 to +.29, delayed roughly +.71 to +.93 (table text partly garbled by OCR, so cell values are approximate). Over half of delayed JOLs sat at the scale ends.
limits: Garbled table. Paired associates, undergraduates.
agent_relevance: Immediate self-ratings carry transient fluency that does not predict outcome. Do not use the confidence emitted with the answer. Re-assess after a gap, in fresh context, or in a separate pass (G5).

source: Rhodes & Tauber (2011) The influence of delaying judgments of learning on metacognitive accuracy: a meta-analytic review
finding: Delayed JOLs are far more accurate in resolution than immediate JOLs. The memory benefit of delay is tiny, so the effect is not mainly a retrieval-practice by-product. Supports the view that delayed JOLs access more diagnostic long-term memory information.
numbers: Meta-analysis 1: 4,554 participants, 112 effect sizes, g = 0.93 on gamma. Meta-analysis 2: 3,807 participants, 98 effect sizes, g = 0.08 on memory.
limits: Abstract via OpenAlex. Cue-match accounts not ruled out. Moderators were not read.
agent_relevance: Largest effect size in this subfield and cheap to use: a delayed, cue-only self-check can be a strong monitor.

source: Benjamin, Bjork & Schwartz (1998) The mismeasure of memory: when retrieval fluency is misleading as a metamnemonic index
finding: Fluency illusion. Predictions of future recall follow how easily and quickly an item was retrieved on an earlier task, even when conditions make early ease negatively related to later recall.
numbers: 3 experiments; predicted and actual performance mismatched strongly (figures not extracted).
limits: Abstract only (via OpenAlex).
agent_relevance: Fluent output is not correct output. Token probability and ease of generation can be high on wrong answers; do not use them as a correctness signal.

source: Koriat & Bjork (2005) Illusions of competence in monitoring one's knowledge during study
finding: Foresight bias. JOLs are made with the answer in view, so they reflect the perceived cue-target association. Later recall depends on the cue-alone association. This creates unwarranted competence at study.
numbers: Paired-associate experiments (numbers not extracted).
limits: Abstract only (via OpenAlex).
agent_relevance: A grader or self-checker that sees the proposed answer is biased the same way. This is the basis for G5: the judge sees no proposed answer.

source: Thompson, Prowse Turner & Pennycook (2011) Intuition, reason, and metacognition
finding: Metacognitive dual-process account. The fast intuitive answer carries a feeling of rightness (FOR) on a continuum. Weak FOR triggers deliberate analysis. Strong FOR lets the intuitive answer stand. FOR is driven by the fluency of the answer and by conflict between responses.
numbers: Several experiments (details not extracted this session).
limits: Full text not opened. Description comes from search summaries and from Gangemi et al.
agent_relevance: A code-side trigger for slow thinking should use signals like conflict among samples and our impasse detector, not a verbalised confidence. Matches G1.

source: Thompson et al. (2013) The role of answer fluency and perceptual fluency as metacognitive cues for initiating analytic thinking
finding: Answer fluency (speed of the first answer) predicts FOR in conditional inference and base-rate problems, and FOR predicts thinking time and answer changes. Perceptual fluency (ease of reading) did not change FOR, retrospective confidence or accuracy across five experiments. People spent longer on hard-to-read items but did not change answers.
numbers: Counts of experiments only. In the last two experiments, perceptual disfluency raised Cognitive Reflection Test accuracy but only for participants of high cognitive ability. No N on the page.
limits: Landing-page summary only, no tables.
agent_relevance: Cheap cue: how fast and how uniformly the first answer arrives. For an LLM, that is agreement among first short samples, not text style.

source: Gangemi, Bourgeois-Gironde & Mancini (2015) Feelings of error in reasoning: in search of a phenomenon
finding: A complementary feeling of error (FOE) arises from conflict detection. Measured by a questionnaire on the bat-and-ball problem. FOE is present when people give the wrong intuitive answer and is diagnostic of genuine error. Also restates the FOR definition from Prowse Turner and Thompson (2009).
numbers: Study 1 (generation) and Study 2 (choose between normative and intuitive answers). Sample sizes not extracted.
limits: Small studies on one problem type. Publication year approximate.
agent_relevance: Error signals from conflict exist before any external check. For us: disagreement between two independent attempts is the conflict signal, computed in code.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language models (mostly) know what they know
finding: Large pretrained models are well calibrated on multiple-choice and True/False questions when options are visible. Calibration improves with size and few-shot prompting. Models can then self-evaluate their own samples as P(True). Showing many of the model's own samples improves self-evaluation. P(IK), trained on TriviaQA, separates answerable from unanswerable questions but is poorly calibrated out of distribution.
numbers: 52B model; five sampling tasks (TriviaQA, Lambada, Arithmetic, GSM8k, Codex) equally weighted in Figure 1. Replacing an option with 'none of the above' lowers accuracy and calibration on MMLU. RLHF policies look badly miscalibrated but one temperature, T=2.5, largely fixes it. OOD P(IK) is mostly underconfident; training on all 4 datasets fixed the Lambada collapse. P(IK) rises with relevant sources and correct hints.
quote: larger k for k-shot self-evaluation seems to primarily help by improving calibration, rather than by improving the AUROC
limits: Anthropic pretrained and early RLHF models of 2022, not frontier models. Exact ECE values live in figures that were not extracted.
agent_relevance: Own P(True) is at most a weak input. The large gain came from comparing many samples, which code can do (G4, G5).

source: Lin, Hilton & Evans (2022) Teaching models to express their uncertainty in words
finding: GPT-3 finetuned on arithmetic (CalibratedMath) learns to output verbalised confidence such as '90% confidence' that is calibrated in distribution and moderately calibrated under distribution shift. It is not a copy of the logit and not a simple heuristic such as integer size.
numbers: Train on add-subtract; test on multi-answer and multiply-divide. In MSE the finetuned verbalised probability generalises better than the zero-shot answer logit and a constant baseline; the indirect logit generalises about as well. A linear probe on pretrained embeddings also works. Meaningless label names worked slightly better than meaningful words.
limits: Table cells garbled in extraction so cell values are omitted. GPT-3 and arithmetic only.
agent_relevance: Verbalised calibration can be trained, but an inference-only scaffold cannot train. Evidence for a code-side recalibration step (fit a map from signal to accuracy on logged results).

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs express their uncertainty? An empirical evaluation of confidence elicitation in LLMs
finding: Verbalised confidence is overconfident and a weak failure predictor. Human-inspired prompts help calibration somewhat. Consistency across several samples helps failure prediction much more. White-box methods are only a little better. No method wins everywhere, and all struggle on professional-knowledge tasks.
numbers: 5 LLMs including GPT-4 and LLaMA 2 Chat. GPT-4 vanilla average AUROC 62.7% (chance 50%). About 22.2% AUROC gain from GPT-3 to GPT-4. GSM8K: AUROC 54.8% with one verbalised answer vs 92.7% with 5 samples plus consistency. GPT-4 with CoT on GSM8K: 93.6% accuracy and ECE 0.064 by giving 100% to every answer. Pair-Rank ECE as low as 0.028; Avg-Conf best on AUROC; white-box vs black-box AUROC 0.605 vs 0.522. Gains from more samples saturate by about M=13.
quote: the model's failure prediction capability is still limited, i.e., close to the performance of random guess
limits: 2023 models. In Table 4 the Avg-Conf aggregator gave AUROC 41.0 on GSM8K vs 84.4 for plain consistency, so the best aggregator varies by task.
agent_relevance: Best evidence for our design: failure prediction comes from sample agreement counted in code. Low ECE can be a trick of near-constant confidence, so always report AUROC beside ECE.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just ask for calibration: strategies for eliciting calibrated confidence scores from language models fine-tuned with human feedback
finding: For RLHF models (ChatGPT, GPT-4, Claude 1 and 2) verbalised confidence is better calibrated than the token probability, often cutting ECE by a relative 50%. Asking for the top-k answers with probabilities improves it (consider the opposite). Chain-of-thought does not help calibration. Llama-2-70B-Chat gains less.
numbers: gpt-3.5-turbo ECE, SciQ: label prob 0.256; verbalised 1-stage top-1 0.234, top-2 0.132, top-4 0.065. TriviaQA: label prob 0.140; verbalised top-2 0.050. TruthfulQA: label prob 0.451; top-4 0.203. 1000 questions each for TriviaQA and SciQ, 817 for TruthfulQA. Verbalised AUC on TruthfulQA at most 0.551, about chance.
limits: Short factual QA. Correctness judged by GPT-3.5 or GPT-4 equivalence checks. Low ECE with poor AUC on hard sets.
agent_relevance: Ask for several candidate answers with probabilities that must share one budget (matches G5 normalisation). Do not add chain-of-thought for calibration.

source: Kuhn, Gal & Farquhar (2023) Semantic uncertainty: linguistic invariances for uncertainty estimation in natural language generation
finding: Semantic entropy: sample several answers, cluster by meaning (bidirectional entailment), compute entropy over the clusters. It predicts correctness better than token-level entropy, lexical similarity and the P(True) baseline, with larger gains at larger model sizes.
numbers: Table 2 (as extracted): CoQA average distinct meanings 1.27 (correct) vs 1.77 (incorrect), AUROC 0.77 (semantic entropy) vs 0.66 (count of distinct answers). TriviaQA 1.89 vs 3.89, AUROC 0.83 vs 0.79. Margin entropy on CoQA with a 13B model: AUROC 0.54.
limits: OPT-family models of 2023 and short free-form answers. Needs an entailment model. Table layout was garbled so row attribution is approximate.
agent_relevance: A code-checkable signal that matches G4 and G5. Uncertainty is measured over meaning classes, so the grouping must be done by code or an independent checker, not by the answering model.

source: Kapoor et al. (2024) Large language models must be taught to know what they don't know
finding: Prompting alone is not enough. Finetuning on a small set of graded answers (about a thousand) with LoRA beats prompting, sampling and zero-shot classifier baselines on ECE and AUROC. Frozen-feature probes suffice on multiple-choice MMLU, but open-ended questions need training through the model. Estimators generalise across models, and a user study shows uncertainty helps human use.
numbers: LLaMA-2 7B and 13B, Mistral 7B and chat variants, open-ended MMLU. Prompting methods' ECE did not improve with a stronger base model; AUROC improved slightly but the best prompted model trails the worst finetuned one. Sampling gives decent calibration but weak discrimination. Verbal elicitation discriminates better but is poorly calibrated even after temperature scaling.
limits: Needs weights and graded data, so not applicable to a pure scaffold on a closed model. Numeric ECE values not extracted.
agent_relevance: If we log graded results from our own runs, a small learned calibrator over code-side features (agreement, check outcomes) is justified. It must win at equal tokens (G7).

source: Yona, Aharoni & Geva (2024) Can large language models faithfully express their intrinsic uncertainty in words?
finding: Defines faithful response uncertainty as the gap between how decisively an answer is stated and the model's intrinsic confidence (consistency across samples). Standard decoding gives decisive answers even when the model is uncertain. Prompting to hedge produces hedges that do not track intrinsic uncertainty.
numbers: Gemini Nano, Pro, Ultra, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 on knowledge QA. Vanilla conditional mean faithful generation (cMFG) is close to 0.5, the value of any strategy that ignores confidence. Punt rate: vanilla 1%, granularity 3%, uncertainty 10%, uncertainty+ 8%. A later passage reports values up to about 0.63 for GPT-4 and 0.7 for Gemini Ultra (context not verified).
limits: 2024 models, knowledge QA only. Gemini Ultra is the judge. Faithfulness is defined by sample consistency, so it is only as good as that proxy.
agent_relevance: Hedging words are not evidence of uncertainty (G10). Read uncertainty from sample consistency in code, not from the tone of the answer.

source: Zhou, Jurafsky & Hashimoto (2023) Navigating the grey area: how expressions of uncertainty and overconfidence affect language models
finding: Epistemic markers in the prompt change model accuracy. High-certainty expressions cut accuracy about 7% relative to low-certainty ones. Factive verbs hurt and evidentials help. In pretraining data certainty markers co-occur with questions and uncertainty markers with answers, so models may imitate usage rather than reflect uncertainty.
numbers: 50 markers injected into prompts; accuracy varied by more than 80% across templates; 7% decrease for high-certainty markers; claiming 100% certainty gave a drastic drop.
limits: GPT-3 family and short QA. Pretraining analysis is correlational.
agent_relevance: Do not tell the agent to be sure or certain, and avoid certainty wording in any critic prompt. Extends G1 and G11.

source: Steyvers et al. (2025) What large language models know and what people think they know
finding: There is a calibration gap and a discrimination gap between model confidence and human confidence in the model's answers. Default explanations make users overconfident, and longer explanations raise confidence without raising accuracy. Matching explanation wording to the model's internal confidence narrows both gaps.
numbers: 301 participants, 40 questions each. 350 questions for GPT-3.5 and PaLM2 (accuracy 55% and 50%); 336 short-answer questions for GPT-4o (63%). Model AUC .751 (GPT-3.5), .746 (PaLM2), .781 (GPT-4o) vs human AUC .589, .602, .592 on default explanations. Low, medium and high certainty wording each shifted human confidence (Bayes factor above 100).
limits: English-speaking crowd sample. Model confidence came from internal probabilities or sampling, not verbal reports.
agent_relevance: A reader of an LLM answer, human or model, judges by explanation length and tone. Keep the final answer short and strip persuasive padding (G11).

source: Pawitan & Holmes (2024) Confidence in the reasoning of large language models
finding: Two confidence measures: persistence when asked to reconsider, and a self-reported score. Persistence correlates with accuracy, but reconsidering often lowers accuracy, sometimes below chance. Self-reported scores sit near the maximum and carry little information. The two measures correlate only marginally.
numbers: GPT-4o, GPT-4-turbo and Mistral on BBH causal judgement (187 questions), formal fallacies (250) and 46 probability puzzles. Mistral accuracy fell to 36% and 32% when it changed its answer. In formal fallacies GPT-4o and GPT-4-turbo gave confidence 100 to every answer. In causal judgement GPT-4-turbo and Mistral claimed 95 in 78% and 86% of cases with no accuracy gain; GPT-4o had 0.60 vs 0.80 accuracy below vs at or above 95 (p=0.0083).
limits: Small question sets. Prompt wording changed the tendency to switch answers.
agent_relevance: Supports G1 and G2: a bare 'are you sure' prompt flips answers, often to wrong ones. Doubt must come from a failing check, not from asking the model.

source: Mielke, Szlam, Dinan & Boureau (2022) Reducing conversational agents' overconfidence through linguistic calibration
finding: Chit-chat models are poorly calibrated linguistically: they state answers confidently even when likely wrong. A separate calibrator that predicts the chance of being correct, plus a controllable generator that conditions phrasing on that probability, greatly improves linguistic calibration.
numbers: Pipeline on open-domain dialogue models with TriviaQA-style questions. Specific ECE numbers were not verified from the text.
limits: 2020-era dialogue model. The calibrator uses model internals, not a closed black box.
agent_relevance: A separate predictor of correctness whose output is injected as a controlled input beats self-report. Same split as the schema: code decides, the model fills a slot.

source: Pleskac & Busemeyer (2010) Two-stage dynamic signal detection: a theory of choice, decision time, and confidence
finding: Evidence keeps accumulating after the choice, and confidence is read from the accumulated evidence by a rating criterion. One process explains choice, response time and confidence, and predicts that resolution improves with more post-decision time. Fits a perceptual and a general-knowledge task.
numbers: Model fits; no single N extracted.
limits: Abstract only (via OpenAlex).
agent_relevance: Time after the first answer is useful. A second look at the same evidence can add resolution the first pass lacks, a parallel to the delayed JOL.

source: Fleming & Daw (2017) Self-evaluation of decision-making: a general Bayesian framework for metacognitive computation
finding: Confidence as a second-order inference on a coupled but separate decision system, like inferring the performance of another actor. Accounts for dissociations where metacognition is better or worse than task performance and unifies confidence and error detection.
numbers: Simulations, no empirical N.
limits: Abstract only (via OpenAlex). The meta-d' metric of Maniscalco and Lau (2012), standard for this, was not opened.
agent_relevance: Design target: the monitor should be a distinct system with its own evidence (checks, extra samples), not the generator grading itself.

source: Hoffrage (2011) Recognition judgments and the performance of the recognition heuristic depend on the size of the reference class
finding: Reported by a secondary search summary: a first experiment testing PMM theory's sampling prediction (random vs selected item sets differ in difficulty) did not support it, and a second experiment that separated difficulty from sampling did. The failure led to the recognition heuristic.
numbers: No counts recorded. Page downloaded but not read.
limits: Boundary condition for PMM; unverified here.
agent_relevance: Item-selection explanations of overconfidence do not always hold; treat as a competing account to test, not a rule.
